CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 29 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/04/2026 - PAGE 10F 4

Commissionets,

I am writing as a utility customer and member of the public concerned about the new “extra-
large-load” tariffs currently proposed by OG&E (PUD 2026-000046) and PSO (PUD
2025-000075). Despite both of Oklahoma’s largest electric utilities having signed onto the
standards called for in the White House’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge (the “White House
Pledge”),' the proposed tariff terms currently under consideration by the OCC don’t meet those
standards in the White House Pledge, which explicitly demands that “U.S. hyperscalers and Al
companies . . . pay[] the full cost of their energy and infrastructure, no matter what.”

OG&E’s and PSO’s proposed tariffs arguably aim to comply only with Oklahoma’s Data Center
Ratepayer Protection Act (“Oklahoma’s Ratepayer Act”).? But Oklahoma’s Ratepayer Act only
protects “residential, commercial and industrial customers ... from paying unjust rates resulting
directly from electric service to large load customers.” In other words, it only requires data
centers to pay the infrastructure costs of connecting their new operations to the grid. The White
House Pledge, on the other hand, goes further and is much more inclusive of the overall
additional costs that data centers cause and should have to pay.

For instance, the White House Pledge provides that data center “[c]ompanies will build, bring, or
buy the new generation resources and electricity needed to satisfy their new energy demands,
paying the fidl cost of those resources whether by building, or buying from, new or otherwise
additive power plants.” And for good measure, “[w]here possible, these companies will also add
more capacity that serves the broader public by increasing supply."

Despite the clear dictates in the White House Pledge, the “Terms and Conditions of Service for
Extra Large Load (XLPL) Customers” in OG&E’s large-load tariff application’ are limited to the
“direct” costs required by Oklahoma’s Ratepayer Act: “XLPL customers will pay 100% of the
costs to connect to the grid,” but “any potential adverse rate impact to other customer rate classes
resulting from the costs of providing service to an XLPL customer, including costs of added
generation or power delivery infrastructure and any fuel, purchased capacity expense, or
purchased power expense, will be reviewed and addressed by the Commission in each general
rate case proceeding,’ meaning the door is left open for some of those costs to be pushed onto

existing residential and commercial customer classes. In other words, OG&EF’s large-load tariff
application is inconsistent with—and falls short of —the standards in the White House Pledge.

Similarly, the new large-load tariff terms in PSO’s proposed final order” mandate new
extra-large-load customers pay “all costs allocated by Section 3 of the [Oklahoma] Ratepayer
Protection Act,” again, again referring only to the “direct” connection costs. Similarly, the terms
of the large-load tariff settlement agreement reached by Google, the OCC Public Utility
Division, the Petroleum Alliance, and the Department of Defense*® simply mirrors the Ratepayer
Act’s “direct” and “directly attributable” language.

These tariff proposals put ratepayers at risk. The problem for ratepayers is that none of the
existing tariff proposals currently mandate that extra-large-load customers pay “the full cost of
.. the new generation resources and electricity needed to satisfy their new energy demands.”

Nor do they mandate that “Companies will pay for a// new power delivery infrastructure
upgrades required to service their data centers, including adequate network upgrade costs,
which is precisely what the White House Pledge requires, Such tariff terms are critical to
protecting OG&E and PSO’s existing customers now and in the future.

3309

Additionally, this Commission has recently preapproved some $3 billion in new generation and
storage capacity projects for OG&E (PUD 2025-000038 and PUD 2025-000084) and PSO (PUD
2025-000064).'° OG&E is also seeking OCC preapproval for three more Capacity Purchase
Agreements (“CPAs”) of undisclosed cost explicitly intended to serve Google data centers (PUD
2026-000031)." Both OG&E and PSO have specifically cited anticipated demand from new
data centers to demonstrate the “need” required for preapproval of these significant new capacity
expansions. The OCC also approved CWIP (“Construction Work in Progress”) financing for
some projects, meaning existing customers begin paying for the new projects’ construction costs
before anyone actually sees any benefit from them. Consequently, it appears current customers
of OG&E and PSO are already paying for hundreds of millions of dollars of capacity and
infrastructure improvement costs that these utilities have pledged would be paid by the new data
centers themselves. Again, this is inconsistent with the White House Pledge, to the detriment of
ratepayers across the state.

Moreover, OG&E, PSO and Governor Stitt committed to the White House that data center
companies “will pay these rates for the power and related infrastructure that are brought online to
service their data centers, whether they use the electricity or not.”'? Nevertheless, the large-load
settlement under consideration in PSO’s rate case” only requires Google to pay a portion of any
costs for unused electricity and does not include an obligation to pay for “related infrastructure.”
Again, this is inconsistent with the White House Pledge’s clear language requiring Google to pay
for all unused electricity and related infrastructure. Likewise, OG&E’s proposed tariff terms
similarly set minimum billing charges at less than a data center’s contracted demand."

In short, while I expect attorneys for data centers will argue that under Oklahoma’s Ratepayer
Act, data centers are only required to pay for added costs resulting directly from their new
operations, those minimum cost-allocation standards do not comply with the requirements of the
White House Pledge that Oklahoma’s largest electric utilities and data center companies like
Google, Amazon, xAI, Meta, and Core Scientific all signed.'¢

Congress and other states have also moved to enact broader consumer protections for ratepayers
that the Oklahoma Corporation Commission should strive to match. For instance, bi-partisan
proposed federal legislation requires states to consider adopting a standard that “recover[s] from
the large-load customer the fill, incremental cost of any generation, transmission, or distribution
upgrade necessary to serve the load of such large-load customer.”'? Similarly, Utah now
requires large-load customers to pay for “large load incremental costs” and ensure those costs are
excluded from general rates."

Importantly, the bi-partisan congressional “large-load” legislation is not limited to data centers.
Its provisions would protect existing customers from costs caused by any customers contracting
for electricity of “100 megawatts or more at a single site or campus.”"” Thus, if the OCC
approves tariff terms adopting Congress’s proposed standards, existing PSO customers would
also be protected from costs caused by the proposed aluminum smelter in Inola, projected to use
1,000 MW all by itself.2° There is no reason PSO’s existing customers should not similarly be

protected from electricity bill increases caused by large industrial users like the proposed smelter,

When it filed for its new large-load tariff, OG&E issued a press release proclaiming that under
the utility’s proposed terms, “Large-load users like data centers would cover all their costs.””! As
things stand, that statement is, at best, inaccurate and misleading. However, the OCC can and
should hold the utilities accountable for their public pronouncements and make their consumer
protection pledges a reality.

Simply put, the Oklahoma Corporation Commission should adopt new tariff terms that mandate
the standards that OG&E, PSO and the data center companies have already voluntarily agreed to
in the White House Pledge by requiring extra-large-load customers to pay for ail of their
incremental costs— both direct and indirect.

Thank you for your consideration.

Respectfully, Ae
Nick Coffey
